citations.quote: **(i) The two-label central model.** A model of class (i) is a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$ labels, fixed masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_0$, the collision-excluded configuration domain $$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$ for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and the force map presented through the time-independent **static central pair potential** $$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),\qquad u:J_0\to\mathbb R\ \text{of class }C^2,$$ so that $F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain (clauses (iii) and (iv) of [[post-cm02-interactions]]; $U$ is of class $C^2$ on the open $Q$ by [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). In the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of that postulate the model has $F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$: no external forces act on the labels of a model of class (i).

4. **(Reconstruction and bijection.)** The identities $x_1=X+\frac{m_2}{M}r$ and $x_2=X-\frac{m_1}{M}r$ hold on $J$. Conversely, if $X^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is affine with $(X^{\circ})''=0$ and $r^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is a $C^2$ curve with $\lvert r^{\circ}(t)\rvert\in J_0$ and $\mu(r^{\circ})''=-u'(\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert)r^{\circ}/\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert$ on $J$, then $$x_1^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}+\frac{m_2}{M}r^{\circ},\qquad x_2^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}-\frac{m_1}{M}r^{\circ}$$ define a motion $x^{\circ}:J\to Q$ of the model whose centre of mass is $X^{\circ}$ and whose relative coordinate is $r^{\circ}$. Consequently the assignment $x\mapsto(X,r)$ is a bijection from the motions of the model on $J$ onto the pairs (affine curve $X^{\circ}$ with $(X^{\circ})''=0$\!, central-force trajectory $r^{\circ}$ for $(\mu,u)$ with values in $J_0$) on $J$.

The curve $r$ is a **central-force trajectory for** $(\mu,U)$ when $$\mu\,r''(t)=-\frac{U'(|r(t)|)}{|r(t)|}\,r(t)\qquad(t\in I),$$ where $|x|:=\lVert x\rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and $U'$ is the derivative of $U$ on the open interval $J_0$. **Attached objects.** The **angular momentum vector** of such a trajectory is the curve $j:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $$j(t):=\mu\,r(t)\times r'(t),$$ with $\times$ the cross product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); its **energy** is the function $E:I\to\mathbb R$, $$E(t):=\tfrac12\mu\,\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2+U(|r(t)|);$$ and for every $J\ge0$ the **effective potential of momentum magnitude** $J$ is the function $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J:J_0\to\mathbb R$, $$U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho):=U(\rho)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu\,\rho^2}.$$

**(a) Unconstrained branch.** The **unconstrained configuration domain** is an open set $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, chosen as part of the model. A tuple $x\in Q$ is an **admissible configuration**: an assignment of one position to each label at one time. A **singular-force exclusion** is the removal of the **collision set** $$\Delta:=\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:\ \text{there are }i\ne j\text{ with }x_{i}=x_{j}\Bigr\}$$ from the domain, which is done when the model's force law is not defined at coincident positions: $\Delta$ is closed (it is the union of the finitely many closed sets $\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}$, each the zero set of the continuous map $x\mapsto x_{i}-x_{j}$), so $Q:=\mathbb R^{3N}\setminus\Delta$ is open and is a legitimate configuration domain.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that $t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and $$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$ Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to D$ is a solution of the associated first-order system on $J$.

Let $\mu>0$, let $U:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$, let $R>0$ satisfy $U(r)=0$ for every $r\ge R$, let $E>0$ and $J>0$, and put $V(r):=U(r)+J^2/(2\mu r^2)$ ([[def-cm-scattering-data]]). Suppose $r_*>0$ satisfies $$V(r_*)=E,\qquad V'(r_*)<0,\qquad V(r)<E\quad(r>r_*).$$ Let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with constant nonzero angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, energy $E$, and $|r(t)|\ge r_*$ for all $t\in I$, whose radial part attains the value $r_*$ at some $t_*\in I$ ([[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]). Then: 1. $(\rho')^2=\dfrac{2}{\mu}\bigl(E-V(\rho)\bigr)$ on $I$, where $\rho=|r|$; $\rho'(t_*)=0$ and $\rho''(t_*)=-V'(r_*)/\mu>0$, so $t_*$ is a strict minimum of $\rho$; 2. $r$ extends uniquely to a central-force trajectory on all of $\mathbb R$; along the extension $\rho\ge r_*$, $\rho(t)>\rho(t_*)=r_*$ for $t\ne t_*$, and $\rho$ is strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,t_*]$ and strictly increasing on $[t_*,\infty)$; 3. the time quadrature $$\tau(r):=\int_{r_*}^{r}\frac{\mathrm ds}{\sqrt{(2/\mu)(E-V(s))}} \qquad(r\ge r_*)$$ is finite for every $r$ and satisfies $\rho(t_*+\tau(r))=r$ for all $r\ge r_*$; 4. for every time $t_1\ge t_*$ with $\rho(t_1)>R$ the motion is exactly free from $t_1$ on: $r(t)=r(t_1)+(t-t_1)r'(t_1)$ for all $t\ge t_1$, and $\rho$ is strictly increasing there; symmetrically, for $t_2\le t_*$ with $\rho(t_2)>R$, $r(t)=r(t_2)+(t-t_2)r'(t_2)$ for all $t\le t_2$.

Let the hypotheses of [[thm-cm-scattering-turning-point-and-global-branches]] hold, with finite-range potential $U$, energy $E>0$, angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, outer turning point $r_*$, and let $r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be the extension of the trajectory. Then: 1. the limits $v_\pm:=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r'(t)$ exist and satisfy $|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}$; 2. for every $t_2\le t_*$ with $\rho(t_2)>R$, the incoming branch is the straight line $\{r(t_2)+s\,v_-:s\in\mathbb R\}$; its perpendicular distance from the origin is $$b:=\frac{|r(t_2)\times v_-|}{|v_-|}=\frac{J}{\mu|v_-|}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad J=\mu b|v_-| .$$

Then: 1. the half-angle $$\Delta:=\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{J\,\mathrm dr}{r^2\sqrt{2\mu\,(E-V(r))}}$$ is finite and positive, and $$\theta(\infty)-\theta(t_*)=\Delta=\theta(t_*)-\theta(-\infty),\qquad \theta(\infty)-\theta(-\infty)=2\Delta;$$ 2. $\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}n(\theta(t))$ exist and equal $v_+/|v_+|$ (as $t\to+\infty$) and $-v_-/|v_-|$ (as $t\to-\infty$); 3. consequently $$\frac{v_+}{|v_+|}=-R_{2\Delta}\Bigl(\frac{v_-}{|v_-|}\Bigr), \qquad \frac{\langle v_-,v_+\rangle}{|v_-|\,|v_+|}=-\cos 2\Delta=\cos(\pi-2\Delta);$$ in particular, if $0<\Delta<\pi/2$ then $\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi)$ is the (undirected) angle between the asymptotic velocity directions, and the signed velocity rotation is $-( \pi-2\Delta)$ in the orientation defined by $e_3$.

Let $(a_1,a_2)\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an interval with at least two points, let $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ be of class $C^1$ with $\theta'(b)\ne0$ for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$ — a deflection branch with inverse $b:(\theta_1,\theta_2)\to(a_1,a_2)$ in the sense of [[def-cm-scattering-data]] — and let $g:(0,\pi)\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and $2\pi$-periodic in its second argument. Then $$\int_{a_1}^{a_2}\!\int_0^{2\pi} g\bigl(\theta(b),\varphi\bigr)\,b\;\mathrm db\;\mathrm d\varphi =\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}\!\int_0^{2\pi} g(\theta,\varphi)\,b(\theta)\,\bigl|b'(\theta)\bigr|\;\mathrm d\theta\;\mathrm d\varphi .$$ Consequently the outgoing angular measure carried to the branch has density $b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|$ with respect to $\mathrm d\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi$, and cross-section density $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta) =\frac{b(\theta)\,\bigl|b'(\theta)\bigr|}{\sin\theta} =\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'(b(\theta))\bigr|}\qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2)$$ with respect to the solid-angle element $\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi$; the two expressions agree because $b'(\theta)=1/\theta'(b(\theta))$. For finitely many branches with pairwise disjoint images the contributions add.

**Deflection branch.** A **deflection branch** is an interval $(a_1,a_2)\subseteq(0,\infty)$ with at least two points together with a function $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ that is of class $C^1$ and satisfies $\theta'(b)\ne0$ for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$. Such a $\theta$ is strictly monotone and its image is an interval with endpoints $\theta_1<\theta_2$ ([[def-interval]]); its inverse $b:(\theta_1,\theta_2)\to(a_1,a_2)$ is differentiable with $b'(\theta)=1/\theta'(b(\theta))$, by the derivative-of-an-inverse theorem [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]] applied to the continuous injective $\theta$ (every point of $(a_1,a_2)$ is a limit point of it, [[def-limit-point-r]], [[def-derivative]]). **Cross-section density.** The **cross-section density of the branch** is the function $$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(\theta):=\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'\bigl(b(\theta)\bigr)\bigr|} \qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2).$$

**(i) The differential cross-section of a branch.** Let a central scattering model be given, let $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ be a **deflection branch** in the sense of [[def-cm-scattering-data]] — an interval $(a_1,a_2)$ of impact parameters with $\theta$ of class $C^1$ and $\theta'(b)\ne0$ — and suppose the branch **records the deflection** of the model: for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$ the scattering motion of the model with impact parameter $b$, energy $E$ and angular momentum $J$ has scattering angle $\theta_{\mathrm{s}}=\theta(b)$. Write $(a_1,a_2)\ni b\mapsto\theta\in(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ for this bijection and $b(\theta):=\theta^{-1}(\theta)$ for its inverse ([[def-cm-scattering-data]]). The **differential cross-section of the branch** is the function $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta):=\frac{b(\theta)\,\bigl|b'(\theta)\bigr|}{\sin\theta} =\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'\bigl(b(\theta)\bigr)\bigr|}\qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2),$$ the cross-section density of [[def-cm-scattering-data]].

**(iv) The uniform-incident preparation (adopted model datum).** The **uniform-incident preparation** of a central scattering model with cutoff $b_{\max}>0$ and flux $\Phi>0$ is the following adopted model of a scattering experiment for the reduced problem: independent incident reduced labels, each with energy $E>0$, angular momentum $Je_3$ and impact-azimuth pair distributed with density $b\,\mathrm db\,\mathrm d\varphi$ on $(0,b_{\max})	imes(0,2\pi)$ normalised to unit total mass, where the **incident flux** $\Phi$ is the number of incident labels per unit area per unit time and $[\Phi]=\ell^{-2}	au^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). Under this preparation the model predicts the expected rate $$\dot N(A)= \Phi\cdot
u(A)$$ of incident labels whose impact-azimuth pair lies in $A$, where $
u$ is the incident flux measure of [[def-cm-scattering-data]]; the rate of scattered labels into a solid-angle set is the flux times the pushforward of $
u$ under the deflection map, whose density on a branch is the cross-section density introduced in this page's cross-section definition.
For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$. This is the right-handed **cross product**.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The **Euclidean norm** of $x$ is $$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$ which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and [[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by [[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function $$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$ the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ ([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives $x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$. $f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is $$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$: | | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms | |---|---|---|---| | $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ | | $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ | | $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ | | $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ | | | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is **closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$, $[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

### Limits, for a real domain Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$, let $c$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) and let $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$. We say $f(x)$ **tends to $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$**, and write $\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$, when $$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ 0 < |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ \lVert f(x) - L\rVert_2 < \varepsilon\ \bigr].$$ This is the condition of [[def-function-limit]] with the absolute value in the codomain replaced by $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$; as there, the puncture $0 < |x-c|$ is what makes $c$ a point the function need not be defined at, and the hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is what stops the condition from being satisfied vacuously.

derivations.claim: The relative coordinate is a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$ with attached angular momentum $j=Je_3$ and energy $E$ by [L1], of class $C^2$ with values $|r(t)|\in J_0=(0,\infty)$; thus $r$ satisfies all hypotheses of the finite-range scattering theorems [L2] with the data $(\mu,u,R,E,J,r_*)$: $U=u$ is $C^2$ on $(0,\infty)$, $U(r)=0$ for $r\ge R$ by (H1), $V(r_*)=E$ with $V'(r_*)<0$ and $V(r)<E$ for $r>r_*$ by (H2), and the trajectory attains the value $r_*$ at $t_*\in J_0$ while satisfying $|r|\ge r_*$.

Clause 1: [L2] gives that $r$ extends uniquely to a central-force trajectory $\bar r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\rho\ge r_*$, $\rho(t)>r_*$ for $t\ne t_*$, $\rho$ strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,t_*]$ and strictly increasing on $[t_*,\infty)$, and the quadrature identity. For the model statement, let $X$ be the centre of mass of the original motion, affine on $J_0$ with $X''=0$ by [L1] clause 2, and let $\bar X$ be its affine extension to $\mathbb R$; then by [L1] clause 4 the pair $(\bar X,\bar r)$ reconstructs a motion of the model on all of $\mathbb R$ with relative coordinate $\bar r$ and centre of mass $\bar X$, because $|\bar r(t)|\in J_0$ for all $t$ (so the configuration remains admissible) and the force presentation is the same. This is clause 1.

Clause 2, asymptotic velocities: by [L2] the limits $v_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}\bar r'(t)$ exist with $|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}=v_\infty>0$, and for every $t_1\ge t_*$ with $\rho(t_1)\ge R$ one has $\bar r(t)=\bar r(t_1)+(t-t_1)\bar r'(t_1)$ for $t\ge t_1$, with $\bar r'(t_1)=v_+$; the incoming statement is symmetric.

Clause 3: by [L2] the half-angle identity $\theta(+\infty)-\theta(t_*)=\Delta=\theta(t_*)-\theta(-\infty)$ holds with $\Delta$ the displayed finite positive quadrature, and the directional identities $v_+/|v_+|=-R_{2\Delta}(v_-/|v_-|)$ and $\langle v_-,v_+\rangle/(|v_-||v_+|)=\cos(\pi-2\Delta)$ hold; hence $\theta_{\mathrm s}=\arccos(\cos(\pi-2\Delta))$ by the definition of $\theta_{\mathrm s}$ in [[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]] clause (iii), and if $0<\Delta<\pi/2$ then $\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi)$ is that angle, the signed velocity rotation being $2\Delta-\pi$. This is clause 3.

Clause 2, impact parameter: on the incoming branch choose $t_2\le t_*$ with $\rho(t_2)\ge R$; the incoming line is $\{\bar r(t_2)+s\,v_-:s\in\mathbb R\}$ and its perpendicular distance from the origin is $|\bar r(t_2)\times v_-|/|v_-|=|j|/(\mu|v_-|)=J/(\mu v_\infty)$ by [L2] clause 2 and [L4]. For the outgoing line $\{\bar r(t_1)+s\,v_+:s\in\mathbb R\}$, the same computation with [L4] gives distance $|\bar r(t_1)\times v_+|/|v_+|=|j|/(\mu|v_+|)=J/(\mu v_\infty)$; since $J/(\mu\sqrt{2E/\mu})=J/\sqrt{2\mu E}$, both distances equal $b=J/\sqrt{2\mu E}$ as displayed, and multiplying by $v_\infty$ gives $J=\mu b v_\infty$.

Clause 4: by the branch hypothesis the model's scattering angle at impact parameter $b\in(a_1,a_2)$ equals $\theta(b)$, and $\theta$ is a deflection branch with inverse $b(\theta)$; [L3] then gives the displayed double-integral identity and the density statements, the cross-section density agreeing with the definition of [[def-cm15-cross-section]] clause (i). For the expected rate, the uniform-incident preparation assigns incident flux measure $\nu$ with density $b$ on $(0,b_{\max})\times(0,2\pi)$ and the model predicts the rate $\Phi\,\nu(A)$ of labels with impact-azimuth data in $A$ and, for the branch, the pushforward rate into the window $Y=(\theta(a_1),\theta(b_{\max}))$; expressing that pushforward through the density of [L3] and converting the polar measure $\mathrm d\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi$ into the solid-angle element gives $\Phi\sigma(Y)$ with $\sigma$ as displayed in [[def-cm15-cross-section]] clause (iii). This is clause 4.

Clause 5 is the statement of the scope: the branch hypothesis of clause 4 is an explicit assumption, not a consequence of (H1)-(H2); no monotonicity or nonvanishing of $\theta'$ off the branch is used or claimed; and the exclusions are those of [[post-cm05-central-model]] clause (v) together with (H1). This completes the proof.

boundaries.evidence: The branch interval is nondegenerate by the definition of a deflection branch, and step 3.2 applies the area pushforward on it; no possibly empty family is quantified.
$E>0$ and $J>0$ exclude the zero-energy and radial cases in step 1.1, and the branch derivative is nonzero by hypothesis in step 3.2.
One relative coordinate, one apsis and one branch in clause 4; step 3.1 computes the single number $b=J/\sqrt{2\mu E}$ on both asymptotes.
The simple outer turning point $V'(r_*)<0$ of (H2) is checked in step 1.1, and stationary deflections $\theta'(b)=0$ are excluded from the branch in step 3.2.
The improper endpoint $r_*$ of the quadrature is finite by clause 1 (step 2.1); the branch image endpoints are excluded from the density and the cutoff may equal the upper endpoint (step 3.2).

citations.quote: Let $\mu>0$, let $\kappa>0$ and $U(r)=\kappa/r$ on $(0,\infty)$ (the repulsive Coulomb potential, of class $C^2$), let $E>0$ and $J>0$, and put $$V(r):=\frac{\kappa}{r}+\frac{J^2}{2\mu r^2},\qquad b:=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}>0,\qquad \alpha:=\frac{\kappa}{Eb}>0.$$ Then: 1. $V$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, with $V(r)\to\infty$ as $r\downarrow0$ and $V(r)\to0$ as $r\to\infty$; hence there is exactly one $r_*>0$ with $V(r_*)=E$, it is simple ($V'(r_*)<0$), and $V(r)<E$ for all $r>r_*$. 2. Let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with constant angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, energy $E$, with $|r(t)|\ge r_*$ for all $t\in I$ and with $|r(t_*)|=r_*$ for some $t_*\in I$. Then $r$ extends uniquely to all of $\mathbb R$; along the extension $\rho=|r|\ge r_*>0$ (no collision), $\rho$ is strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,t_*]$ and strictly increasing on $[t_*,\infty)$, and the asymptotic velocities $v_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r'(t)$ exist with $|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}$. Moreover the asymptotic perpendicular distance of each branch to its limiting direction exists and equals $$b=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}=\frac{J}{\mu|v_\pm|}, \qquad\text{so that}\qquad J=\mu b|v_\pm| .$$ 3. For the polar angle, with $u_*:=1/r_*$, $$\Delta:=\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{J\,\mathrm dr}{r^2\sqrt{2\mu\,(E-V(r))}} =\int_0^{u_*}\frac{b\,\mathrm du}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{\kappa}{E}u-b^2u^2}} =\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$

**(i) The two-label central model.** A model of class (i) is a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$ labels, fixed masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_0$, the collision-excluded configuration domain $$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$ for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and the force map presented through the time-independent **static central pair potential** $$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),\qquad u:J_0\to\mathbb R\ \text{of class }C^2,$$ so that $F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain (clauses (iii) and (iv) of [[post-cm02-interactions]]; $U$ is of class $C^2$ on the open $Q$ by [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). In the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of that postulate the model has $F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$: no external forces act on the labels of a model of class (i).

4. **(Reconstruction and bijection.)** The identities $x_1=X+\frac{m_2}{M}r$ and $x_2=X-\frac{m_1}{M}r$ hold on $J$. Conversely, if $X^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is affine with $(X^{\circ})''=0$ and $r^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is a $C^2$ curve with $\lvert r^{\circ}(t)\rvert\in J_0$ and $\mu(r^{\circ})''=-u'(\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert)r^{\circ}/\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert$ on $J$, then $$x_1^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}+\frac{m_2}{M}r^{\circ},\qquad x_2^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}-\frac{m_1}{M}r^{\circ}$$ define a motion $x^{\circ}:J\to Q$ of the model whose centre of mass is $X^{\circ}$ and whose relative coordinate is $r^{\circ}$. Consequently the assignment $x\mapsto(X,r)$ is a bijection from the motions of the model on $J$ onto the pairs (affine curve $X^{\circ}$ with $(X^{\circ})''=0$\!, central-force trajectory $r^{\circ}$ for $(\mu,u)$ with values in $J_0$) on $J$.

Suppose the two **material balance identities** $$m'(t)=r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t),\qquad (mv)'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)$$ hold for every $t\in I$, where $mv$ denotes the pointwise scalar multiple. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function $$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$ the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ ([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives $x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$. $f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is $$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

Let $N\ge1$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), let $m_1,\dots,m_N>0$ and let $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable at every point of $I$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The **Euclidean norm** of $x$ is $$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$ which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and [[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by [[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Limits, for a real domain Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$, let $c$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) and let $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$. We say $f(x)$ **tends to $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$**, and write $\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$, when $$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ 0 < |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ \lVert f(x) - L\rVert_2 < \varepsilon\ \bigr].$$ This is the condition of [[def-function-limit]] with the absolute value in the codomain replaced by $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$; as there, the puncture $0 < |x-c|$ is what makes $c$ a point the function need not be defined at, and the hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is what stops the condition from being satisfied vacuously.

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$: | | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms | |---|---|---|---| | $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ | | $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ | | $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ | | $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ | | | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is **closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$, $[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

**(i) Particle labels and worldlines.** A model of the framework has **particle labels** $i=1,\dots,N$ for some $N\ge1$. To each label and each *inertial frame* of the model — an adapted chart $(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}))$ with coordinates $(t,x)$ in the sense of [[post-cm01-frames]] — there is assigned a **worldline** $\gamma_{i}:I\to A$ described in that frame, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nondegenerate open interval — that is, an interval of the form $(a,b)$ with $-\infty\le a<b\le+\infty$ and at least two points — the curve $\gamma_{i}$ is of class $C^{2}$ in the adapted coordinates of the frame, and the **parameter condition** $$\tau\bigl(\gamma_{i}(t)-o\bigr)=t\qquad(t\in I)$$ holds: the curve parameter is the elapsed time from the origin of the frame, so in the frame's coordinates $\gamma_{i}(t)=(t,x_{i}(t))$ with $x_{i}:I\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{2}$. The parameter condition replaces the causal conditions of relativistic kinematics: no timelike condition on the velocity and no upper bound on its Euclidean norm is imposed, and the parameter is not free up to reparametrization.

**(d) Dimensions of the quantities of this framework.** The dimension map is fixed on the following quantities: 1. coordinates: $[t]=\tau$ and $[x_{i}]=\ell$; 2. velocity components: $[w_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$; 3. acceleration components: $[a_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-2}$; 4. mass: $[m]=\mu$, and the mass operator (multiplication of spatial components by masses) has dimension $\mu$; 5. angles and entries of rotation matrices: dimensionless, $[R_{ij}]=1$ for $R\in SO(3)$ under the radian convention, in which an angle is the ratio of an arc length to a radius and therefore a ratio of two lengths; 6. the standard derived quantities have the dimensions obtained from the rules of (b) once their defining relations are stated: momentum $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$, force $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, energy $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$, action $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$, angular momentum $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$;

**(a) Unconstrained branch.** The **unconstrained configuration domain** is an open set $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, chosen as part of the model. A tuple $x\in Q$ is an **admissible configuration**: an assignment of one position to each label at one time. A **singular-force exclusion** is the removal of the **collision set** $$\Delta:=\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:\ \text{there are }i\ne j\text{ with }x_{i}=x_{j}\Bigr\}$$ from the domain, which is done when the model's force law is not defined at coincident positions: $\Delta$ is closed (it is the union of the finitely many closed sets $\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}$, each the zero set of the continuous map $x\mapsto x_{i}-x_{j}$), so $Q:=\mathbb R^{3N}\setminus\Delta$ is open and is a legitimate configuration domain.

**(i) The isolated reciprocal impulse model.** A two-label force model with masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), time window $I_0$, configuration domain $Q$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]) and continuous external-plus-pair force maps $F_1,F_2$ is **run in the isolated reciprocal impulse model at $t_*\in I_0$** when there is a motion $x=(x_1,x_2):I\to Q$ of the associated first-order system ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]) such that: 1. $x_1,x_2$ are continuous on $I$ and twice continuously differentiable on each of $I\cap(-\infty,t_*)$ and $I\cap(t_*,\infty)$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and $m_ix_i''(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ for every $t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}$; 2. the one-sided limits $v_i^{\pm}:=\lim_{t\to t_*\pm}x_i'(t)$ exist in $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); 3. there is a vector $J\in\mathbb R^3$, the **impulse**, with $$m_1\bigl(v_1^+-v_1^-\bigr)=J,\qquad m_2\bigl(v_2^+-v_2^-\bigr)=-J .$$ The two equations of clause 3 are the **reciprocal finite-jump form** of the isolated impulse: the two labels receive equal and opposite momentum changes. The model places no bound on the force maps across $t_*$; its distributional rendering by test-function pairings is proved in [[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]]. The dimension of the impulse is $[J]=\mathsf M\ell\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

derivations.claim: Clause 1: by [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (i) and [L1], $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=J$ and $m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=-J$; adding gives $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)+m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=0$, which is exactly $P(t_*^+)=P(t_*^-)$. This is clause 1.

Clause 2: let $x$ be a smooth-branch motion with continuous force maps along it. By [L3] the curves $x_i''=F_i/m_i$ are continuous, hence $x_i$ is $C^2$ and $p_i=m_ix_i'$ is $C^1$ on $I$; a $C^1$ function on an interval has equal one-sided limits at every interior point, so $p_i(t_*^+)=p_i(t_*^-)$ and therefore $J=0$. Thus the model of clause (i) with $J\ne0$ is outside this class, as asserted.

Clause 3: the collinear contact satisfies the hypotheses of [L1] on the relative velocity, so [L1] gives $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=J=-m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)$ and the displayed velocities with $V$ the centre-of-mass velocity; since $v_2^--v_1^-\parallel n$ and $J=\mu(1+e)(v_2^--v_1^-)$ is a scalar multiple of it, $J\parallel n$. The explicit identity $J=\mu(1+e)(v_2^--v_1^-)$ follows from the two jump equations and the restitution law: subtracting the second from the first, $v_2^+-v_1^+=(v_2^--v_1^-)-\frac{J}{\mu}$, which by the restitution law equals $-e(v_2^--v_1^-)$, so $J=\mu(1+e)(v_2^--v_1^-)$.

Clause 4: [L1] gives the kinetic-energy change $-\frac{1-e^2}{2}\mu\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2$, which is $\le0$ because $0\le e\le1$, and vanishes exactly when $e=1$ or $v_2^-=v_1^-$ (if $e<1$ and $v_2^-\ne v_1^-$ it is strictly negative). The identification statement is a statement of the scope of the model: the deficit is computed from the contact law, and no measured observable of another framework is introduced or equated with it. This is clause 4.

Clause 5: fix any real $J_n\le\mu d_n$ and put $v_1^+:=v_1^-+\frac{J_n}{m_1}n$, $v_2^+:=v_2^--\frac{J_n}{m_2}n$; then $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=J_nn$ and $m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=-J_nn$, so the reciprocal impulse equations of clause 1 hold with impulse $J=J_nn$, and adding the two equations shows that the total momentum is preserved. The relative velocity becomes $d^+=d^--\frac{J_n}{\mu}n$; hence $d^+\cdot n=d_n-\frac{J_n}{\mu}\ge0$ precisely for $J_n\le\mu d_n$, which is the stated admissibility (the contact separates or grazes). By the kinetic identity [L4], $\Delta K(J_n)=\frac{\mu}{2}\bigl(\lVert d^+\rVert_2^2-\lVert d^-\rVert_2^2\bigr) =\frac{\mu}{2}\bigl(-2\frac{J_n}{\mu}d_n+\frac{J_n^2}{\mu^2}\bigr) =-J_nd_n+\frac{J_n^2}{2\mu}$, a quadratic in $J_n$ with minimum $\frac{\mu}{2}d_n^2$ at $J_n=\mu d_n$; the restitution law selects $J_n=\mu(1+e)d_n$, which lies in the admissible range because $1+e\ge1$ and $d_n<0$, and reproduces clause 3.

Clause 6: [L2] gives the derived law from the material balance identities, and the three special cases are its substitutions: (a) $r_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$ leaves $mv'=F$, while $(mv)'=m'v+mv'=F$ because $m'=0$; (b) $r_{\mathrm{in}}=0$, $r_{\mathrm{out}}=-m'$ gives $mv'=F-r_{\mathrm{out}}(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)=F+r_{\mathrm{out}}(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})$; and $(mv)'=m'v+mv'=F+r_{\mathrm{out}}(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})+m'v=F-r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}+r_{\mathrm{out}}v-r_{\mathrm{out}}v=F-r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}$, which equals $F$ exactly when $w_{\mathrm{out}}=v$ (or $r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$); (c) $r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$, $w_{\mathrm{in}}=0$ gives $mv'=F-r_{\mathrm{in}}v$, while $(mv)'=m'v+mv'=r_{\mathrm{in}}v+F-r_{\mathrm{in}}v=F$. This is clause 6.

The perfectly inelastic value $e=0$ is included; step 1.3 handles every $e\in[0,1]$ and step 1.4 records that the energy change vanishes exactly at $e=1$ or $v_2^-=v_1^-$.
One impulse vector $J$ and one contact direction $n$; step 1.1 pairs the two momentum changes through the single $J$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), inherited from the statement of [[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]], whose distributional jump lemma uses it; declared in the Statement and carried by the citation of step 1.1.
Clause 4's equality case is an equivalence: step 1.4 proves $\Delta K\le0$ and the exact vanishing condition $e=1$ or $v_2^-=v_1^-$.
The converse of the vanishing case is the same equivalence, established in step 1.4 through the factor $(1-e^2)\mu\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2/2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport theorem. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, let $\chi$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]) with spatial velocity $u$, let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ be an open set containing the swept region

$$\Sigma:=\bigl\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\bigr\}.$$

Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); call it a **density field**. A **material subregion** is a nonempty bounded open $B'\subseteq B$ with $\overline{B'}\subseteq B$ ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]); for such $B'$ the same $\chi$ is a motion of $B'$.

**(i) Localization.** Assume for every material subregion $B'$ and every $t\in J_0$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)\,dx=0, \tag{CM}$$

It is sufficient to assume this identity only for those pairs $(t,B')$ for which $\chi_t(B')$ is an open Euclidean ball with closure inside $\chi_t(B)$. Under either version of the conservation hypothesis,

$$\partial_t\rho(t,x)+\operatorname{div}\bigl(\rho u\bigr)(t,x)=0$$

for every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$, with the material derivative and divergence of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]].

**(ii) Converse.** Conversely, if $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ on an open neighbourhood of $\Sigma$ in $U$, then (CM) holds for every material subregion $B'$ and every $t\in J_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport and divergence theorems. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, let $\chi$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$ and material derivative $D_t$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]], [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]), let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$, and let $U$ contain the swept region $\Sigma=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\}$.

Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ be a $C^1$ density field, let $\sigma:U\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^1$ field (the stress field of [[def-cm-traction-and-stress]]), and let $b:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Suppose:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)u(t,x)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)b(t,x)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(B')}\sigma(t,y)\,\nu(y)\,dS(y),$$

where $\nu$ is the outward unit normal and the surface integral is that of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]].

A **traction field** is a map $$t:S^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,$$ read with the following convention: $t(n)$ is the force per unit area exerted **by the material on the side towards which $n$ points upon the material on the other side**, at the point of a surface whose unit normal is $n$. The dependence of $t$ on position and time is suppressed in this notation; a traction **field on a set** $\Omega\times I$ is a map $t:\Omega\times I\times S^2\to\mathbb R^3$, and all statements below apply to each fixed $(y,s)$. A matrix $\sigma\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]) **represents** the traction field $t$ when $$t(n)=\sigma n\qquad\text{for every }n\in S^2,$$ the product being matrix-vector multiplication ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport and divergence theorems. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, let $\chi$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$, let $J_0\subseteq I$ have compact closure in $I$, and let $U$ contain the swept region of $B$ over $\overline{J_0}$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]).

Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ and $\sigma:U\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be $C^1$ and let $b:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Define $g_i:=\sum_j\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$ and suppose, on $U$:

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\rho\,D_tu=\rho b+g . \tag{KM}$$

Let $\psi:I\times O'\to\mathbb R^3$ be a second motion of a material region $B'\subseteq B$ (with the same reference chart domain $O'=O$ used for $B$; write $w$ for its spatial velocity), and suppose that for every $t\in J_0$ the control region $C_t:=\psi_t(B')$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]) with outward unit normal $\nu$ and boundary surface integral as in [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]].

Assume also that the control sweep $\Sigma_C:=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\psi_t(\overline{B'})\}$ is contained in $U$. Thus the fields and the local equations (KM) are defined on a neighbourhood of every closed control region. No condition that the control motion coincide with the material motion is imposed.

Then for every $t\in J_0$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{C_t}\rho\,dx=-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,dS, \tag{CV1}$$

and componentwise

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{C_t}\rho u_i\,dx=\int_{C_t}\rho b_i\,dx+\Bigl(\int_{\partial C_t}\sigma\nu\,dS\Bigr)_i-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho u_i\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,dS\qquad(i=1,2,3). \tag{CV2}$$

A **motion of $B$ on $I$** consists of an open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $\overline B\subseteq O$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) together with a map $$\chi:I\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3$$ such that: 1. $\chi$ is of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); 2. for every $t\in I$ the map $\chi_t:=\chi(t,\cdot):O\to\mathbb R^3$ is of class $C^1$, is injective, and has $D_X\chi_t(X)$ invertible for every $X\in O$; 3. writing $$J(t,X):=\det\bigl(D_X\chi_t(X)\bigr)$$ with the determinant of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]], one has $J(t,X)>0$ for every $(t,X)\in I\times B$. We call $X\in B$ the **material label** (reference position), $x=\chi(t,X)$ the **position** at time $t$ of the label $X$, and $$\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$$ the **current (material) region** at time $t$. Condition 2 makes each $\chi_t:O\to\chi_t(O)$ a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto the open set $\chi_t(O)$ ([[cor-injective-regular-ck-map-is-a-ck-diffeomorphism-onto-its-image]]). The **spatial velocity field** of the motion is $$u:\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,\qquad u\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr):=\partial_t\chi(t,X),$$ and the **spatial acceleration field** is the material derivative of $u$ in the sense of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]], $$a(t,x):=D_tu(t,x)=\partial_tu(t,x)+Du(t,x)u(t,x).$$

A bounded $C^1$ domain is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid change of coordinates, the graph $z=h(y)$ of a $C^1$ function, with $\Omega$ locally exactly the subgraph $z<h(y)$. Connectedness is not required. The outward normal in these coordinates is $\nu=(-Dh,1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$, transported by the orthogonal coordinate map. Its overlap agreement is justified with surface charts below.

Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]]. For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]), let $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and let $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be maps. Suppose the two **material balance identities** $$m'(t)=r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t),\qquad (mv)'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)$$ hold for every $t\in I$, where $mv$ denotes the pointwise scalar multiple. Then $$m(t)v'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in I).$$ In particular, if $F\equiv0$, $r_{\mathrm{in}}\equiv0$ and $r_{\mathrm{out}}\equiv r$ for a constant $r\ge0$, then $mv'=-r(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$: the acceleration is governed by the momentum carried away per unit time relative to the body, not by $(mv)'=0$. The two balance identities are the **adopted content of the material momentum accounting** — the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,dt$ of matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,dt$ with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$". They are not derived here from any closed-system law; the deduction below is their product-rule consequence.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define $$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$ Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$ the **centre of mass** and $\rho_{i}$ the **relative position** of label $i$. The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). derivations.claim: Reflection and conservation: by [L1], $|v^+|=|v^-|=v_\infty$ and the angular momentum about the centre is conserved across the contact; hence the two free pieces of the motion are straight lines and the motion has a constant angular momentum $j$ with $|j|=\mu b v_\infty$, so the impact parameter of the incoming line is indeed $b=J/(\mu v_\infty)$ in the sense of [[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]] clause (ii).

Deflection: let $\alpha$ be the acute angle between the inward normal $-n$ at first contact and the incoming direction $\hat u$, so that $\sin\alpha=b/a$ by [L2]. The reflection turns the velocity by the angle computed in [L2], namely $\pi-2\alpha$; since $b\in(0,a)$ we have $\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$ and $\theta=\pi-2\alpha\in(0,\pi)$.

Branch and inverse: the map $b\mapsto\theta(b)=\pi-2\arcsin(b/a)$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,a)$ by [L3] and its image is $(0,\pi)$; solving $\sin((\pi-\theta)/2)=b/a$ gives $b(\theta)=a\cos(\theta/2)$ on $(0,\pi)$, which is $C^1$ with $b'(\theta)=-\frac{a}{2}\sin(\theta/2)\ne0$. Thus the model realises a single deflection branch with image $(0,\pi)$, and no branch sum is needed for it.

Cross-section density: by [L4], $\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta)=\frac{b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|}{\sin\theta} =\frac{a\cos(\theta/2)\cdot\frac{a}{2}\sin(\theta/2)}{\sin\theta}$. Using $\sin\theta=2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)$ this equals $\frac{a^2}{4}$ for every $\theta\in(0,\pi)$: the outgoing angular distribution is uniform, and the density is finite, positive and independent of $\theta$.

Truncated total: by [L4] and the fundamental theorem, for the full image interval $$\sigma\bigl((0,\pi)\bigr)=\int_0^{\pi}\frac{a^2}{4}\,2\pi\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{a^2}{4}\cdot2\pi\cdot\bigl[-\cos\theta\bigr]_0^{\pi} =\frac{a^2}{4}\cdot 4\pi=\pi a^2,$$ and for $0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\pi$ the band value is $\frac{a^2}{4}\cdot2\pi(\cos\theta_1-\cos\theta_2)$, finite; in particular the branch has a finite ideal total $\pi a^2$.

Then the momentum curves $p_i=m_ix_i'$ are of class $C^1$ on $I$; in particular $$p_i(t_*^+)=p_i(t_*^-)\qquad(i=1,2),$$ so $J=0$: no motion of that class carries a nonzero isolated impulse. citations.quote: **(iii) The open-body material accounting.** Adopt for a body whose mass, velocity, external force and exchanged matter are described by maps $m:I\to(0,\infty)$, $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ (mass rates and *inertial* velocities of the matter entering and leaving, measured in the same inertial frame as $v$) the **material balance identities** $$m'=r_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad (mv)'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}\,w_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}\,w_{\mathrm{out}} .$$ They are the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,\mathrm dt$ of matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,\mathrm dt$ with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$", and they are adopted rather than derived from a closed-system law. Their product-rule consequence $mv'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$ is proved in [[thm-cm-variable-mass-momentum-balance]]; in particular the closed-system law $(mv)'=F$ is recovered only when $r_{\mathrm{in}}w_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}$. The model parameters $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}},w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}$ are model data with $[r_{\mathrm{in}}]=[r_{\mathrm{out}}]=\mathsf M\tau^{-1}$ and $[w_{\mathrm{in}}]=[w_{\mathrm{out}}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]), let $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and let $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be maps. Suppose the two **material balance identities** $$m'(t)=r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t),\qquad (mv)'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)$$ hold for every $t\in I$, where $mv$ denotes the pointwise scalar multiple. Then $$m(t)v'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in I).$$ In particular, if $F\equiv0$, $r_{\mathrm{in}}\equiv0$ and $r_{\mathrm{out}}\equiv r$ for a constant $r\ge0$, then $mv'=-r(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$: the acceleration is governed by the momentum carried away per unit time relative to the body, not by $(mv)'=0$. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function $$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$ The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives $x - c \ne 0$. **The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so $$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$ and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So $q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines. $f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the **derivative of $f$ at $c$** is $$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport and divergence theorems.
**Adopt the smooth open-flow model** with the following model data
([[def-cm-continuum-motion]], [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]],
[[post-cm01-worldlines]], [[def-cm01-units]]): a nonempty open interval $I$;
a material region $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ (bounded open with $C^1$ boundary);
a motion $\chi$ of $B$ on $I$ of class $C^2$ whose time slices are
diffeomorphisms with positive Jacobian onto their images; a density field
$\rho>0$ of class $C^1$ and a spatial velocity field $u$ (the velocity of
$\chi$); a stress field $\sigma$ of class $C^1$
([[def-cm-traction-and-stress]]); and a continuous body-force density $b$;
all fields defined on a neighbourhood of the swept region over a compact
subinterval $J_0$ with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$. Adopt as the model's
**material balances**: for every material subregion $B'\subseteq B$ (a
nonempty bounded open subset with $\overline{B'}\subseteq B$ whose images
$\chi_t(B')$ are bounded $C^1$ domains,
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]) and every
$t\in J_0$,

$$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho\,\mathrm dx=0,\qquad \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho u\,\mathrm dx=\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho b\,\mathrm dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(B')}\sigma\nu\,\mathrm dS,$$

with $\nu$ the outward unit normal and the surface integral that of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. These two balance
laws are **adopted model assumptions** of this item, in the sense of the
open-body accounting of [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (iii); they are not
derived from the particle postulates. Then, for every second motion $\psi$ of
a material region $B'\subseteq B$ on $I$ (the **control motion**) with
control regions $C_t:=\psi_t(B')$ that are bounded $C^1$ domains for
$t\in J_0$, spatial velocity $w$, and outward unit normal $\nu$.
Require its closed sweep $\Sigma_C:=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\psi_t(\overline{B'})\}$ to lie in the common open field domain. Require also either that this sweep lie locally inside the current material region $\chi_t(B)$, where localization supplies the local mass and momentum equations, or that those same local equations $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ and $\rho D_tu=\rho b+g$ be explicitly adopted on a neighbourhood of the control sweep. The control motion need not coincide with $\chi$. Then:

1. **(Control-volume identities.)** For every $t\in J_0$,
   $$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\int_{C_t}\rho\,\mathrm dx =-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS, \tag{CV1}$$
   and componentwise
   $$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\int_{C_t}\rho u_i\,\mathrm dx =\int_{C_t}\rho b_i\,\mathrm dx+\Bigl(\int_{\partial C_t}\sigma\nu\,\mathrm dS\Bigr)_i -\int_{\partial C_t}\rho u_i\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS\qquad(i=1,2,3). \tag{CV2}$$
2. **(Material and fixed special cases.)** If $\psi=\chi$ (the control region
   is material, $w=u$ on the boundary), the flux terms vanish and (CV1),
   (CV2) reduce to the adopted material balances; if $\psi$ is the constant
   motion ($w=0$, $C_t=C$ fixed), then
   $$m_C'=-\int_{\partial C}\rho\,u\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS,\qquad P_C'=\int_C\rho b\,\mathrm dx+\int_{\partial C}\sigma\nu\,\mathrm dS-\int_{\partial C}\rho u\,(u\cdot\nu)\,\mathrm dS$$
   with $m_C:=\int_C\rho$, $P_C:=\int_C\rho u$; the last term is the momentum
   flux through the fixed boundary, and the relation is the fixed-region
   steady-flow balance of the engineering treatment when the fields are
   steady and the region fixed.
3. **(Inlet/outlet decomposition and the open-body law.)** Suppose that for
   every $t\in J_0$ the boundary decomposes into finitely many $C^1$ pieces,
   among which $\Sigma_{\mathrm{in},t}$ (where $(u-w)\cdot\nu<0$),
   $\Sigma_{\mathrm{out},t}$ (where $(u-w)\cdot\nu>0$) and the zero-flux rest,
   and put
   $$r_{\mathrm{in}}:=-\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{in},t}}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS\ge0,\qquad r_{\mathrm{out}}:=\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{out},t}}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,\mathrm dS\ge0,$$
   $$w_{\mathrm{in}}:=\frac{1}{r_{\mathrm{in}}}\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{in},t}}\rho u\,\bigl(-(u-w)\cdot\nu\bigr)\mathrm dS,\qquad w_{\mathrm{out}}:=\frac{1}{r_{\mathrm{out}}}\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{out},t}}\rho u\,\bigl((u-w)\cdot\nu\bigr)\mathrm dS$$
   (the flux averages are used only where the corresponding rate is
   positive), and write
   $$m:=\int_{C_t}\rho\,\mathrm dx>0,\qquad P:=\int_{C_t}\rho u\,\mathrm dx,\qquad F_{\mathrm{ext}}:=\int_{C_t}\rho b\,\mathrm dx+\int_{\partial C_t}\sigma\nu\,\mathrm dS .$$
   Then the control-volume identities read
   $$m'=r_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad P'=F_{\mathrm{ext}}+r_{\mathrm{in}}\,w_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}\,w_{\mathrm{out}},$$
   and the lumped body with mass $m$ and velocity $v:=P/m$ satisfies
   $$m\,v'=F_{\mathrm{ext}}+r_{\mathrm{in}}\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v\bigr),$$
   the derived law of [[thm-cm-variable-mass-momentum-balance]]. In
   particular, a body that only loses mass ($r_{\mathrm{in}}=0$,
   $r_{\mathrm{out}}=-m'$) has thrust
   $r_{\mathrm{out}}(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})=-m'(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})$, and a body
   whose boundary moves with the material ($w=u$; no flux) has
   $m'=0$ and $P'=F_{\mathrm{ext}}$.

   models of the open flow, exactly as clause (iii) of
   [[post-cm15-impulse]] adopts the lumped accounting; this item proves only
   the two stated deductions (localization followed by the control-volume
   identities, and the inlet/outlet reading). It asserts no constitutive law
   for $\rho$ or $\sigma$, no boundary condition, no incompressibility, no
   smoothness beyond the stated one, and no empirical claim; the fields,
   the control motion and the region are model data.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport and divergence theorems. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, let $\chi$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$, let $J_0\subseteq I$ have compact closure in $I$, and let $U$ contain the swept region of $B$ over $\overline{J_0}$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]).

Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ and $\sigma:U\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be $C^1$ and let $b:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Define $g_i:=\sum_j\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$ and suppose, on $U$:

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\rho\,D_tu=\rho b+g . \tag{KM}$$

Let $\psi:I\times O'\to\mathbb R^3$ be a second motion of a material region $B'\subseteq B$ (with the same reference chart domain $O'=O$ used for $B$; write $w$ for its spatial velocity), and suppose that for every $t\in J_0$ the control region $C_t:=\psi_t(B')$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]) with outward unit normal $\nu$ and boundary surface integral as in [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]].

Assume also that the control sweep $\Sigma_C:=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\psi_t(\overline{B'})\}$ is contained in $U$. Thus the fields and the local equations (KM) are defined on a neighbourhood of every closed control region. No condition that the control motion coincide with the material motion is imposed.

Then for every $t\in J_0$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{C_t}\rho\,dx=-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,dS, \tag{CV1}$$

and componentwise

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{C_t}\rho u_i\,dx=\int_{C_t}\rho b_i\,dx+\Bigl(\int_{\partial C_t}\sigma\nu\,dS\Bigr)_i-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho u_i\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,dS\qquad(i=1,2,3). \tag{CV2}$$

A **motion of $B$ on $I$** consists of an open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $\overline B\subseteq O$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) together with a map $$\chi:I\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3$$ such that: 1. $\chi$ is of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); 2. for every $t\in I$ the map $\chi_t:=\chi(t,\cdot):O\to\mathbb R^3$ is of class $C^1$, is injective, and has $D_X\chi_t(X)$ invertible for every $X\in O$; 3. writing $$J(t,X):=\det\bigl(D_X\chi_t(X)\bigr)$$ with the determinant of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]], one has $J(t,X)>0$ for every $(t,X)\in I\times B$. We call $X\in B$ the **material label** (reference position), $x=\chi(t,X)$ the **position** at time $t$ of the label $X$, and $$\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$$ the **current (material) region** at time $t$. Condition 2 makes each $\chi_t:O\to\chi_t(O)$ a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto the open set $\chi_t(O)$ ([[cor-injective-regular-ck-map-is-a-ck-diffeomorphism-onto-its-image]]). The **spatial velocity field** of the motion is $$u:\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,\qquad u\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr):=\partial_t\chi(t,X),$$ and the **spatial acceleration field** is the material derivative of $u$ in the sense of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]], $$a(t,x):=D_tu(t,x)=\partial_tu(t,x)+Du(t,x)u(t,x).$$

The **divergence** of $v$ at $a$ is $$\operatorname{div}v(a):=\operatorname{tr} igl(Dv(a) igr)=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\partial_iv_i(a),$$ the trace of the total derivative ([[def-trace-of-a-square-matrix]]), read in the standard basis of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]). For a $C^1$ scalar field $f:O	o\mathbb R$ and $a\in O$, the **gradient** $
abla f(a)\in\mathbb R^3$ is the vector of partial derivatives of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; it is the unique vector with $Df(a)h=\langle
abla f(a),hangle_2$ for every $h\in\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-gradient-represents-directional-derivatives-and-steepest-ascent]]). We write $\langle
abla f(a),v(a)angle_2=:
abla f(a)\cdot v(a)$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $u:O	o\mathbb R^3$ and $f:I	imes O	o\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. For $(t,x)\in I	imes O$ define the partial time derivative $\partial_tf(t,x):= rac{d}{ds} ig|_{s=t}f(s,x)$ and the **material derivative** of $f$ along $u$ $$D_tf(t,x):=\partial_tf(t,x)+Df(t,x) igl(u(x) igr)=\partial_tf(t,x)+
abla f(t,x)\cdot u(x).$$ For a $C^1$ vector field $w:I	imes O	o\mathbb R^3$ the material derivative $D_tw$ is defined componentwise, and $\operatorname{div}w(t,x)$ means the divergence of $x\mapsto w(t,x)$ at $x$ at each fixed $t$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]), let $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and let $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be maps. Suppose the two **material balance identities** $$m'(t)=r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t),\qquad (mv)'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)$$ hold for every $t\in I$, where $mv$ denotes the pointwise scalar multiple. Then $$m(t)v'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in I).$$ In particular, if $F\equiv0$, $r_{\mathrm{in}}\equiv0$ and $r_{\mathrm{out}}\equiv r$ for a constant $r\ge0$, then $mv'=-r(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$: the acceleration is governed by the momentum carried away per unit time relative to the body, not by $(mv)'=0$. The two balance identities are the **adopted content of the material momentum accounting** — the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,dt$ of matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,dt$ with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$". They are not derived here from any closed-system law; the deduction below is their product-rule consequence.

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$: | | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms | |---|---|---|---| | $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ | | $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ | | $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ | | $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ | | | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is **closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$, $[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$.

citations.quote: **(i) The isolated reciprocal impulse model.** A two-label force model with masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), time window $I_0$, configuration domain $Q$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]) and continuous external-plus-pair force maps $F_1,F_2$ is **run in the isolated reciprocal impulse model at $t_*\in I_0$** when there is a motion $x=(x_1,x_2):I\to Q$ of the associated first-order system ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]) such that: 1. $x_1,x_2$ are continuous on $I$ and twice continuously differentiable on each of $I\cap(-\infty,t_*)$ and $I\cap(t_*,\infty)$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and $m_ix_i''(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ for every $t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}$; 2. the one-sided limits $v_i^{\pm}:=\lim_{t\to t_*\pm}x_i'(t)$ exist in $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); 3. there is a vector $J\in\mathbb R^3$, the **impulse**, with $$m_1\bigl(v_1^+-v_1^-\bigr)=J,\qquad m_2\bigl(v_2^+-v_2^-\bigr)=-J .$$ The two equations of clause 3 are the **reciprocal finite-jump form** of the isolated impulse: the two labels receive equal and opposite momentum changes. The model places no bound on the force maps across $t_*$; its distributional rendering by test-function pairings is proved in [[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]]. The dimension of the impulse is $[J]=\mathsf M\ell\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). **(ii) The collinear restitution contact law.** A model run in the isolated reciprocal impulse model at $t_*$ is **collinear** when there is a unit vector $n\in\mathbb R^3$ (the **contact direction**) with $v_i^{\pm}\parallel n$ for $i=1,2$ and $\langle v_2^--v_1^-,n\rangle<0$ (the labels approach along $n$). For a collinear contact, adopt a **coefficient of restitution** $e\in[0,1]$ — a dimensionless model datum of the pair and the contact — and the **restitution law** $$v_2^+-v_1^+=-e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr).$$ For $e=1$ the contact is called **elastic**, for $e=0$ **perfectly inelastic** and otherwise **semi-elastic**; the law is a constitutive assumption, not a consequence of the impulse equations of clause (i), and $e$ is not derived from the masses or the approach speed. The law is stated only for a single collinear contact; simultaneous contacts, repeated contacts and tangential (friction) impulses are outside the model.

**(ii) Scattering motions and their data.** Let $r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$ defined on all of $\mathbb R$ with values $|r(t)|\in J_0$ and with constant angular momentum $j=\mu\,r\times r'=Je_3\ne0$ for $J>0$ and an oriented orthonormal triad $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ ([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]], [[thm-cm-central-force-angular-momentum-conservation]], [[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]], [[lem-cm-oriented-orthonormal-triads]]). Call $r$ a **scattering motion** of the model when it satisfies the hypotheses under which the page's scattering theorems establish the limits below. Its **energy** is the constant $$E:=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+u(\lvert r\rvert)>0$$ of [[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]] (constant by [[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]] clause 4), its **asymptotic velocities** are the limits $$v_-:=\lim_{t\to-\infty}r'(t),\qquad v_+:=\lim_{t\to+\infty}r'(t),$$ taken in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]] (their existence under the hypotheses is a theorem, not a convention), and its **scattering speed** is $$v_\infty:=\lVert v_-\rVert_2=\lVert v_+\rVert_2=\sqrt{2E/\mu},$$ the equality being part of the scattering theorems. The **incoming branch** is the trajectory restricted to times before its apsis; the **impact parameter** is the perpendicular distance from the force centre of the line through the incoming branch, defined by $$b:=\frac{\lVert r(t)\times v_-\rVert_2}{\lVert v_-\rVert_2} \qquad(t\ \text{on the incoming branch}),$$ with $\times$ the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; the value is independent of $t$ because $r\times r'=j/\mu$ is constant, and the scattering theorems identify it with the geometric distance, giving $b=J/(\mu v_\infty)$. Its dimension is $[b]=\ell$. **(iii) Polar advance and deflection conventions.** Fix polar data $(\rho,\theta)$ of the scattering motion in the triad, $r=\rho\,n(\theta)$, $n(\varphi):=\cos\varphi\,e_1+\sin\varphi\,e_2$ ([[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]), and let $t_*$ be an apsis time, $|r(t_*)|=\min_t|r(t)|$. The **polar advance of one half** is $$\Delta:=\theta(+\infty)-\theta(t_*)=\theta(t_*)-\theta(-\infty),$$ defined by the limits asserted in the scattering theorems, and the **polar advance of the motion** is $2\Delta$. The **scattering angle** is the undirected angle between the asymptotic velocity directions, $$\theta_{\mathrm{s}}:=\arccos\!\left(\frac{\langle v_-,v_+\rangle}{\lVert v_-\rVert_2\,\lVert v_+\rVert_2}\right)\in[0,\pi],$$ equivalently the angle between the incoming and outgoing asymptote lines; the **signed velocity rotation** is the continuous rotation angle of $r'(t)$, measured counterclockwise about $e_3$ relative to the incoming direction, so that a positive value is a counterclockwise turn. The scattering theorems give $\cos\theta_{\mathrm{s}}=\cos(\pi-2\Delta)$ and the signed rotation $2\Delta-\pi$; in particular, when $0<\Delta<\pi/2$ the scattering angle is $$\theta_{\mathrm{s}}=\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi),$$ while for $\Delta\ge\pi/2$ the motion has wrapped past the backward direction and $\theta_{\mathrm{s}}$ is the wrapped value $\arccos(\cos(\pi-2\Delta))$.
For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$. This is the right-handed **cross product**.

Their principal inverses are denoted $$\arcsin:[-1,1]\to[-\pi/2,\pi/2],\qquad\arccos:[-1,1]\to[0,\pi],$$ and are characterised by $$\sin(\arcsin y)=y,\qquad\cos(\arccos y)=y\qquad(-1\le y\le1).$$ The chosen target intervals are part of the notation: without them, inverse sine and inverse cosine would be multivalued relations rather than functions. Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]), let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and differentiable at every point of $I$ interior to $I$ ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]). The words *nondecreasing*, *increasing*, *nonincreasing* and *decreasing* are those of [[def-monotone-function]], in which *increasing* is the strict notion. 1. If $f'(x) \ge 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is nondecreasing on $I$. 2. If $f'(x) > 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is increasing on $I$. 3. If $f'(x) \le 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is nonincreasing on $I$. 4. If $f'(x) < 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is decreasing on $I$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]], [[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$ Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with $g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite $f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable ([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$ at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then: 1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$; 2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$; 3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$; 4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$
